item.title: Valo to deliver 1.6 GWh battery storage system using Wärtsilä GridSolve technology
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: Awarded the contract to deliver the 400 MW / 1,600 MWh Teebar Battery Energy Storage System in Queensland, new energy storage integrator Valo will deploy over 440 containerised batteries for project owner Atmos Renewables.
item.content:encoded:
Born from a joint venture (JV) between Finnish energy tech giant Wärtsilä and German engineering company RCT Solutions GmbH, Valo combines Wärtsilä’s storage technology and software with RCT Solutions’ engineering and manufacturing expertise.

Valo enters the Australian market with over 7.5 GWh across 10 utility-scale energy storage projects in the country, and over 20 GWh globally. It has been selected to deliver for Atmos Renewables the recently announced 400 MW / 1,600 MWh Teebar Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) in Queensland.

One of the largest battery energy storage system projects currently committed for construction in Queensland, Valo will deploy over 440 containerised batteries using Wärtsilä’s GridSolve Quantum2 technology.

Valo Australia Managing Director Suraj Narayan told pv magazine the GridSolve Quantum2 features just over 4 MW in each enclosure and 444 of them will be delivered to Tee Bar.

“Of course, 1,600 MWh is what we contract to demonstrate during a performance test, but we have more than that in store to plan for calendar degradation, losses in the system, and things like that, so it will be oversized,” Narayan said.

“They are LFP batteries, which is the same technology deployed in all of our projects.”

Teebar is also designed to be a grid forming BESS, the GridSolve Quantum2 batteries will be able to respond quickly to market movements.

“They’re very fast in responding, so grid forming means you don’t have to wait for an external, you can sense the change in frequency and respond to it,” Narayan said.

“More and more grid forming in the future will support more introduction of renewables, which is good.”

Valo will also deploy the GEMS proprietary software at the Teebar project.

“We believe the GEMS software is one of the leading systems in the market. It’s basically intelligent controls and optimisation. GEMS is both a power plant controller (PPC) and energy management system (EMS) in one system, so it’s a complete platform,” Narayan said.

“The advantages are that the software is designed in such a way that it responds quickly, and it talks the same language, whereas if you have two different systems from separate suppliers, for example, this can create issues such as time lags, and response times and things not working properly for flow of information.”

“That shows in our performance in all the projects we’ve done here in Australia or globally, you will never hear of any of our projects getting stuck in commissioning due to delays, and these sorts of things.”

Narayan said a key reason for this is that systems are developed in-house.

“We have a big software team in the United States, and we have local resources to support it, so it’s all in-house knowledge, not a bought in product, and it’s been evolved over the last 15 years and is now in its 8th generation.”

One of the challenges to build the Teebar site, which is located approximately 300 kilometres north of Brisbane in the Fraser Coast region, is remoteness.

“It’s not like building a project close to Newcastle for example, that is close to roads and infrastructure. Tee Bar is a more challenging location; it’s quite far and probably will need upgrades on roads, that sort of thing,” Narayan said.

“And because this 1.6 GWh project requires 440-plus containers of batteries and 130-plus inverters, there will be a lot of transportation, and a lot of trucks have to travel between the port to site, so logistics is a big issue with these projects that needs to be managed properly.”

“Our delivery capability is proven, however. We’ve done a lot of projects in Australia successfully and on time and that experience comes through and it’s these things Atmos has considered when selecting Valo; the delivery capability and the performance of our systems on the grid here.”

Facing a two-year build time until operational, Narayan said there’s still going to be a lot of demand for BESS in the near future, based on the pipeline seen today, and projects that are being planned and forecasts being put out.

“But we are a continent of only 26 million people, so demand for the space will saturate at some point, but there’s a lot of talk about data centres having to bring their own power and if that takes off there could be sustained demand for BESS, otherwise, I believe in the next four or five years demand will start tapering off.”

“As coal steps out there has to be more renewables to replace that and when that happens there’s more variability coming into the grid, so you need more balancing technologies.”

Teebar’s lifescycle is 20 years.

“Atmos develop and hold projects for the long term, which means they have to have a quality project, and I believe that’s one of the reasons they selected Valo because we believe in quality and we’re not the cheapest, but you can rely on our solutions and our design commitments,” Narayan said.

item.title: Large-scale solar sets annual financial investment decision record at 3.5 GW+
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: The latest Clean Energy Regulator data shows investment in solar is setting a new annual record with solar final investment decisions for the September 2026 quarter at 1 GW, adding to 3.5 GW already achieved in 2026.
item.content:encoded:
The latest Clean Energy Regulator (CER) data shows investment in solar is setting a new annual record with final investment decisions (FID) for the September quarter sitting at 1 GW, following 2 GW in Q2, adding to the year’s already tallied 3.5 GW, and is approximately 30% above the previous annual solar FID record.

2.1 GW of total large-scale renewable capacity reached FID in the September quarter, which is an equal highest quarterly result, and brings total renewable FID to October 2026 to 5 GW.

That is higher than the previous full-year record of 4.9 GW and brings large-scale FID totals to almost 17 GW since 2022. 

Rooftop solar added 90,042 installations and 894 MW of capacity in the September quarter, which is 35% higher than in Q3 2025, and year-to-date rooftop solar capacity is 45% higher than at the same point in October 2025.

Rooftop solar installations in Q3 were 39% higher than Q3 2025, and has so far added 2.8 GW in 2026, which almost matches the whole of 2025, with three months to go.

Q2 2026 was the biggest rooftop solar capacity quarter on record at 1 GW, and over 13 GW of small-scale solar has been installed since 2022.

Approved capacity under the Cheaper Home Batteries Program (CHBP) reached 15.3 GWh by the end of September, up 1.9 GWh in Q3, and up from less than 2 GWh at the same time in 2025, with total home battery capacity in Australia now more than 5 times greater than when the scheme began on 1 July 2025.  

Cheaper Home Batteries approved capacity has more than tripled during 2026, growing from 5 GWh at the end of 2025 to 15.3 GWh at the end of Q3. With total home battery capacity, including that installed before the scheme, around 19 GWh, it is more than 5 times greater than when the scheme began. 

New South Wales (NSW) has 5.6 GWh of approved home battery capacity, followed by Victoria and Queensland at about 3.2 GWh each.

The data shows about half of approved battery installations are retrofits to existing solar, while about half are going in with new or upgraded rooftop solar.

Federal Minister for Climate Change and Energy Chris Bowen said more renewable energy reaching final investment decision is “what progress looks like”.

“Renewable investment has already broken the annual record with three months still to go. And it isn’t just investment; last month renewable energy generated more electricity in the national grid than fossil fuels,” Bowen said.

“Investors, as well as Australian households and small businesses, are backing Australian renewable energy because they see a government with a clear policy that is working and we’ll continue to get on with the job.”

item.title: Sunergise partners with Cook Islands to install rooftop solar on public buildings
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: New Zealand solar developer Sunergise has partnered with the Cook Islands Investment Corporation to establish a framework for installing rooftop solar on public buildings across the main island of Rarotonga.
item.content:encoded:
New Zealand solar developer Sunergise has partnered with the Cook Islands Investment Corporation (CIIC) to establish a framework for installing rooftop solar systems on public buildings across the main island of Rarotonga.

Located approximately 5,000 kilometres northeast of Sydney in the South Pacific Ocean, Rarotonga has a population of approximately 11,000 people who are reliant on diesel generators as a primary power source, and like many Pacific islands is sensitive to global shipping delays, fuel price fluctuations and regional supply pressures.

Formalising a rooftop licence agreement is the first step for the solar systems to be progressively installed across existing public assets to generate renewable energy and aid in reducing the island’s dependence on imported fuels.

Beyond clean energy generation, the installations will support the Cook Islands’ sustainability and renewable energy objectives, which include transitioning all 12 inhabited islands from diesel-fuelled generators to clean solar and battery hybrid systems.

Sunergise will also collaborate on educational opportunities it already delivers elsewhere in the Pacific, to inspire the next generation in renewable energy and STEM.

As suitable sites are identified and assessed, the programme will progress in consultation with stakeholders, ensuring installations are practical, safe and aligned with operational requirements.

item.title: Lead-acid battery pilot switched on at Victorian university testing facility
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: New Zealand-based energy storage company ArcActive, in collaboration with Origin Zero, has switched on its lead-acid battery system pilot connected to Deakin University's 7.25 MW microgrid and Origin's virtual power plant.
item.content:encoded:
New Zealand-headquartered energy storage company ArcActive has switched on a lead-acid battery system pilot installed at Deakin University’s Waurn Ponds campus 7.25 MW microgrid battery testing facility.

ArcActive’s system combines its proprietary fabric electrode technology with a bipolar battery architecture to create a new generation of lead-acid batteries, building on lead-acid technology already in use to support critical infrastructure, including telecommunications, hospitals and data centres. 

The system consists of bipolar batteries built as a stack of repeating cells, with each cell layered directly on top of the next. Rather than connecting individual cells using conventional straps and inter-cell connections, a bipolar plate forms the boundary between neighbouring cells while also carrying current directly from one cell to the next, ArcActive said.

The result is a compact, sandwich-like structure in which the electrodes, separators and bipolar plates are arranged as parallel layers.

ArcActive said as current flows directly through the thickness of the battery, it’s more uniformly distributed across the electrode area, reducing electrical resistance compared with traditional lead-acid battery designs.

The stacked construction also allows the electrodes to be maintained under high, uniform compression, which is beneficial for the positive electrode, where compression helps support the active material, reduce shedding and extend cycle life.

Excessive compression of conventional negative electrodes, however, can reduce porosity, restricting electrolyte access and limiting performance.The result is a safe, highly recyclable and long-life energy storage solution, which leverages established lead-acid materials and processes and a practical pathway to cost-effective energy storage at scale.

ArcActive Chief Executive Stuart McKenzie said lead-acid technology is a technology that engineers, approval authorities and insurers already know.

“There are established pathways for approving and insuring these installations, which is an important starting point when you want to put batteries alongside businesses and occupied buildings,” McKenzie said.

“We want businesses to be able to deploy storage through a more standardised, repeatable process, with greater confidence about the cost, the approval requirements and the financial return.”

“The cost of installing a battery goes beyond the battery itself. Businesses also need to account for engineering work, approvals, insurance and safety measures. If they don’t know what their site will need or how much it will cost, they can be reluctant to invest,” McKenzie said.

Supported by Origin Zero and also connected to Origin’s Virtual Power Plant (VPP), the pilot project aims to solve common issue faced by commercial sites like factories, warehouses, and shopping centres, that can benefit from storing cheap solar energy to cut power bills, but are deterred by high upfront costs, complex installation approvals, and insurance hurdles.

Origin Group Manager for Customer Solution Development and Emerging Technology Bill Truscott said trials such as this offered opportunities to learn about emerging technologies and their potential applications for customers.

“We’re interested in how new technologies could help our commercial and industrial customers innovate and manage their energy needs,” Truscott said.

item.title: Scientists develop moth-eye-inspired antireflective surfaces for PV modules
item.dc:creator: Lior Kahana
item.description: Researchers in Portugal have investigated the mechanical durability of moth-eye-inspired antireflective silicon surfaces for photovoltaic applications. They found that repeated sliding causes nanopillar fracture and material compaction, with higher mechanical loads leading to increased friction and wear.
item.content:encoded:
Researchers in Portugal have investigated the friction and wear behavior of moth-eye-inspired silicon surfaces designed to reduce light reflection and improve light absorption in solar cells. The study examined, in particular, how these antireflective nanostructures withstand mechanical stress relevant to solar module operation.

“If we want to integrate these nanostructures into the outer surfaces of photovoltaic modules, we also need to understand how they respond to mechanical contact, cleaning operations, and other environmental challenges,” corresponding author Vítor Lopes told pv magazine.

“Rather than focusing only on optical performance, we investigated how these structures respond to friction and repeated mechanical loading, and how their morphology evolves as damage accumulates.”

Lopes said the team believes that applying a tribological perspective to light-management nanostructures is an important step toward understanding their durability and supporting their development for practical PV applications.

“Coming from a mechanical engineering background and now working in photovoltaic research, I saw an opportunity to approach this problem from a different perspective,” he added.

The researchers fabricated moth-eye-inspired silicon surfaces measuring approximately 2.5 cm × 2.5 cm, with nanopillars averaging 434 nm in height and about 100 nm in diametre. They produced a silicon master mold through reactive ion etching, using gold nanoparticles formed by thermal dewetting as an etching mask. They then replicated the pattern onto an intermediate polymer stamp and imprinted it onto resist-coated silicon wafers using nanoimprint lithography, before transferring the pattern into the silicon through reactive ion etching.

To assess friction and wear, the team slid a 5 mm-diameter steel ball across the patterned surfaces without lubrication, applying loads of 0.1 N and 0.5 N at a sliding speed of 5 mm/s for up to 50 cycles. Each test condition was repeated three times.

The researchers recorded the friction coefficient throughout testing, measured wear-track widths using optical microscopy, and examined nanopillar fracture, collapse, and compaction using scanning electron microscopy (SEM). They also measured initial reflectance across wavelengths of 300 nm to 1,100 nm, but did not assess reflectance after wear testing.

“One of the most interesting findings was that the friction coefficient remained relatively stable under lower mechanical loading, even though SEM images revealed clear structural modifications to the nanostructures,” said Lopes. “This tells us that friction measurements alone may not be enough to assess the integrity of these surfaces.”

After 50 sliding cycles, the average wear-track width reached approximately 252 µm under the 0.1 N load and 388 µm under the 0.5 N load. The friction coefficient ranged from 0.40 to 0.56 under the lower load but exceeded 1.0 by the 50th cycle under the higher load. The researchers also observed changes in wear mechanisms as mechanical loading and the number of sliding cycles increased.

“While the initial damage was mainly characterised by nanopillar fracture, continued sliding led to the accumulation and compaction of fractured material, progressively changing the original surface morphology,” Lopes said. “Under higher loads, this transformation was accompanied by a noticeable increase in friction.”

The findings are presented in Exploring the mechanical resilience of light-management nanostructures: Wear and degradation analysis of silicon moth-eye-inspired surfaces for photovoltaic applications, published in Surfaces and Interfaces. The research team included scientists from Portugal’s International Iberian Nanotechnology Laboratory, the University of Minho, LABBELS – Associate Laboratory, and the University of Aveiro.

From pv magazine Global

item.title: Cheaper industrial decarbonisation linked to shared use of renewables
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: A new report from Monash University’s Climateworks Centre has found industries that coordinate by sharing infrastructure and using electricity more flexibly, require smaller, smarter and cheaper clean energy systems.
item.content:encoded:
A new report from Monash University’s Climateworks Centre has found industries that coordinate by sharing infrastructure and using electricity more flexibly, require smaller, smarter and cheaper clean energy systems.

The collective approach to energy also reduces the cost of systems and electricity prices for industries by 20% compared to a scenario where an industry player transitions its energy alone.

Cost savings are the result of avoiding unnecessary infrastructure build-out, reducing the amount of solar capacity needed by 22%, wind by 9% and battery storage by 50%.

A coordinated approach results in efficiencies that lead to 40% less electricity curtailed and wasted, the report found.

The ‘Strengthening Industrial Prosperity Through Coordinated Energy Planning’ report follows a case study of an industrial precinct energy plan (IPEP) in Central Queensland, using modelling of two pathways for a clean energy transition in Gladstone.

One pathway where companies build their own renewable generation, batteries and supporting infrastructure is compared to a scenario where industries share infrastructure and coordinate when and how they use electricity.

Climateworks Centre Chief Executive Officer Anna Skarbek said the difference is significant.

“Both pathways beat business as usual, and coordination delivers the lowest-cost outcome, with potential electricity savings of up to 50%, outcompeting business-as-usual Queensland grid prices from the early 2030s.”

Using Gladstone as a case study, the research proposes the approach could be rolled out across Australia’s industrial regions including Kwinana, Hunter, Whyalla, and the Pilbara.

Energy Efficiency Council Head of Policy Jeremy Sung said Australia faces a critical decision in determining how to best build the energy infrastructure that will power the nation’s future economy.

“We can choose to build in an uncoordinated way and bear the extra costs, or optimise energy use to deliver infrastructure faster, cheaper and with lower impacts on the environment,’ Sung said.

“A joined-up approach to developing energy infrastructure in Australia’s key industrial hubs makes complete sense.”

Australian Industry Group Director of Climate Change and Energy Tennant Reed said the report helps put industrial energy needs front and centre in electricity system development.

“Reducing what needs to be built through shared infrastructure slashes costs and should unlock faster regulatory approvals too. That’s a good recipe for competitiveness and unlocking growth and energy system planning should take this perspective on board as fast as possible,” Reed said.

Climateworks recommends developing IPEPs to complement national energy planning and establish a shared view of future regional electricity demand and identify the least-cost pathway for generation, storage and transmission, through opportunities for industries to share infrastructure and use energy more flexibly.

item.title: Acciona, GenusPlus, UGL contracted to unlock 2.3 GW of renewable energy in WA
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: Acciona, GenusPlus and UGL Engineering have been selected by the Western Australian government to deliver the state's Clean Energy Link - East transmission line project, which will help unlock the equivalent renewable energy used of a million homes.
item.content:encoded:
Unlocking the equivalent power usage of 1 million homes, or 2.3 GW of renewable energy, Spanish clean energy developer Acciona, Western Australia (WA)-based engineering and construction company GenusPlus, and Sydney-based CIMIC Group’s UGL Engineering have been awarded a major contract to build the Clean Energy Link (CEL) – East transmission project in WA.

The CEL – East will expand the state’s transmission network east of Collie, which is located approximately 200 kilometres south of Perth, to increase access to renewable energy solar and wind projects as state-owned coal fired power stations retire by 2030.

Stage 1 of the project includes new and upgraded transmission lines between Collie and Darkan, connecting renewable energy zones (REZ) in eastern and south-eastern region of the South West Interconnectedc System (SWIS).

Critical infrastructure to be delivered include a new 330 kV terminal at Cordering, expansion of Shotts and Muja terminals, 38 km of 330 kV transmission lines from Shotts to Cordering, and 54 km of 330 kV transmisson lines from Muja to Cordering.

CIMIC Group Chief Executive Officer Jason Spears said as Australia accelerates its transition to a lower-carbon future, the need for large-scale transmission infrastructure has never been greater.

“UGL’s proven ability to deliver complex energy and utility projects, backed by the strength and resources of CIMIC Group, positions us to help customers deliver the networks needed to connect renewable generation and power communities. We are proud to contribute our expertise to this landmark investment in Western Australia’s energy future,” Spears said.

UGL Managing Director Sam Goldsmith said UGL is proud to continue supporting Western Power on one of Western Australia’s largest infrastructure transformations in its history.

“As leaders in critical energy infrastructure, projects like Clean Energy Link – East demonstrate the critical role UGL plays in shaping Australia’s energy future. Drawing on decades of experience delivering complex transmission, power and utility infrastructure, we have the people, technical expertise and integrated delivery capability to successfully execute projects of this scale,” Goldsmith said.

UGL’s contract is approximately $478 million.

Collie-Preston Member of the Legislative Assembly Jodie Hanns said Collie has powered WA for generations, and the CEL – East expansion shows it will keep playing a vital role in our energy system for generations to come.

“The expansion of the Muja and Shotts terminals and the new 330kV transmission lines from both sites will keep Collie at the heart of the South West Interconnected System,” Hanns said.

“As more renewable energy comes online, Collie will continue to play its part in powering homes, businesses and industry across WA.”

Updated 15/10/2026, 2.25pm

item.title: Lack of consumer energy resources retailer memberships skew EWON complaint data
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: The true number of consumer complaints about residential or business rooftop solar or battery energy storage system installations in New South Wales, is hidden from the state’s energy ombudsman due to a lack of retailer memberships.
item.content:encoded:
A lack of consumer energy resources retailer memberships with the Energy & Water Ombudsman NSW (EWON) is impacting consumer protections against faulty household and businesses rooftop solar and battery energy storage systems.

The release of its annual report, indicates consumer energy resource complaints increased from 301 in FY25 to 677 in FY26, however do not tell the full story as EWON does not have jurisdiction over non-member providers.

EWON Ombudsman Janine Young said the organisation can only resolve solar and battery complaints when retailers are EWON members, which limits access for consumers to EWON’s free and independent service.

“Consumers and small businesses deserve a one-stop shop that provides consistent, timely and fair advice and dispute resolution, and EWON is best placed to do this across NSW,” Young said.

“As supported by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) in their June Inquiry into the National Electricity Market (NEM) report, EWON’s long term goal is to have jurisdiction to take complaints about all retailers of solar, battery, virtual power plants (VPP) and electric vehicle (EV) residential charging, so that we can fully address this consumer protection gap.”

EWON received 27,011 complaints across FY26, with 677 consumer energy resources complaints recorded in FY26, showing a jump of 125% or a doubling of complaints year-on-year to FY26.

Of the 677 complaints, 245 regarded system performance, 81, smart energy services, 192, installation and/or connection, 60, CER payment plans, 55, complaint handling and 44, for system activation.

However, complaints about residential and small business rooftop solar and battery sales and installation were a small percentage of the total complaints, which Young said would be higher if EWON had jurisdiction over all related complaints.

“The Commonwealth Government’s Cheaper Home Battery Program (CHBP) is making investment in solar, and home batteries mainstream for many people, and consumer protections need to catch up,” Young said.

Young said access to external dispute resolution is fragmented, with customers getting caught in referral loops, resulting in varying levels of resolution.

“The energy market is transforming, and NSW is leading the way towards a cleaner energy future, but many households still struggle to afford to heat or cool their homes and keep appliances running.,” Young said.

The Ombudsman added that the energy transition reinforces the need for independent dispute resolution and access to home solar and batteries to help customers afford their energy bills.

“The challenges facing consumers today are complex, ranging from rising costs and payment difficulties to new technologies and energy products,” Young said.

Clean Energy Regulator (CER) figures show a national total of 401,185 home batteries had been recorded as installed nationally from 1 July 2025 to 31 May 2026 under the small-scale renewable energy scheme (SRES), and the CHBP, with 175,000 of those in NSW.

As of mid-2026 NSW had over 1.17 million rooftop solar systems installed across all-time, and by October 2026, 4,532,178 rooftop solar installations have been installed on homes and businesses nationally.

EWON ‘s figure of 677 complaints in FY 2026 represent just 0.05% of the combined 1.35 million solar and battery installated in NSW.

item.title: Up the ante on ambition: $250 million Solar Sunshot Round 3 now open
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: The Australian Renewable Energy Agency has opened the $250 million Solar Sunshot Round 3, for local and global companies to develop product, manufacture, or scale-up technology capable of reducing large-scale solar costs and speeding up solar build times in Australia.
item.content:encoded:
Targeting equipment, manufacturing processes and deployment technologies, the Australian Renewable Energy Agency (ARENA) has opened the $250 million (USD 174 million) Solar Sunshot Round 3 inviting Australian and international companies with commercially mature technologies to apply.

Round 3 is focused on the commercial-scale manufacture of solar balance of plant and deployment technologies, which could include racking and tracking systems, robotics, advanced automation, prefabrication and other technologies, and which must contribute to achieving ARENA’s ultra low-cost solar (ULCS) goals, such as the 30-30-30 target to achieve 30% module efficiency at an installed cost of 30 cents per watt by 2030.

ARENA General Manager Solar Dan Sturrock told pv magazine Round 3 signals Australia is open for business with the world’s best solar innovators that want opportunities to develop or manufacture products at scale in Australia. 

“We think the next decade is a really exciting time to bring the best innovation from around the world here to Australia and show those products can be produced at scale to drive down the costs and increase the efficiency of how we build large-scale solar in Australia,” Sturrock said.

“We’re coming out now with Round 3 to be able to extend the ambition already demonstrated through Rounds 1 and 2. Round 2 has been running for about 12 months and we’ve got a couple of projects we’ve been able to announce, plus a strong pipeline of other projects coming through that round, and we expect to fully allocate the $150 million that we made available.”

Sturrock said with SunShot Solar Round 3 ARENA is more ambitious, wanting to work with a broader range of companies but also asking those companies to be equally ambitious with their ability to go larger at scale.

“Not just to manufacture product but to also really focus on product development, because when you think about recent Solar Sunshot Round 2 recipients, Built Robotics and Luminous Robotics, most of the product development happens in the US at the moment, so there’s an opportunity to bring product development expertise to Australia and really think about what’s the right product for this market,” Sturrock said.

Projects and products under Round 3 must also deliver value to the end user the builds or owns utility-scale solar farms.  

“We expect these projects to reduce the cost of solar farms, and it’s also about product quality, so if you’re building a quality product hopefully it’s lower cost but overall we expect these technologies to lower costs in the long term as we build out 10 GW of large-scale solar a year, rather than the current 5 GW.”

“We obviously look at value for money to the taxpayer, ultimately. Applicants do need to bring their own private investment. We generally expect in all of these projects that we’re not funding more than 50% of the total project cost,” Sturrock said.

“Sometimes a project is looking for a capital subsidy to reduce the cost of building a factory and sometimes they’re looking for a production subsidy to make their first batch of whatever the product is, to be cost effective and be able to break into the market at scale.”

“We’re hoping once established successful applicants are not only build a strong business in Australia but there’s absolutely no reason why they shouldn’t then be able to export those products or services to other markets in the region, whether that’s New Zealand, South East Asia, or further afield,” Sturrock said.

“When you look through the short term challenges in lots of different areas, we’re very optimistic that in 10 years’ time the solar industry will have grown massively and there’ll be really big changes in the way we build and operate solar farms in Australia with all the new technologies that are available,” Sturrock said.

Expressions of interest for Solar Sunshot Round 3 open on 2 November 2026.

Solar Sunshot Round 2

ARENA announced on 13 October 2026 Round 2 successful applicants US-based Built Robotics and Luminous Robotics, respectively receiving grants of $14.5 million and $17.8 million to establish new manufacturing facilities.

“Luminous Robotics has only been around for about three years, but they came to us early and received a small amount of funding and then saw a great opportunity to come in and scale up their business in Australia,” Sturrock said.

“They’re a really exciting company, high growth, big ambitions and now looking to manufacture their LUMI robots at scale in Melbourne, and they’re a great example, because we worked with them at the smaller scale when they demonstrated the robots at Goorambat and Culcairn solar farms in the last year or so.”

ARENA also worked with Californian start-up Built Robotics when they came to Australia to test their product.

“Like Luminous they are now seeing a great opportunity to scale up their piling robots in Brisbane and are building a large facility there where they’ve currently just got a small workshop,” Sturrock said.

Solar Sunshot Round 1

Applications for the $50 million Round 1B for upstream solar manufacturing feasibility studies and front end engineering and design (FEED) has been extended to 12 November 2027.

“We’re extending Round 1B to give an opportunity to both new entrants to come to us but also for companies to apply for second stage support. It is a bit of a ‘watch this space’, because we really need to come to an understanding of what does success look like in that upstream space because it is a difficult one and one that is rapidly evolving based on what is going on in the US and China, in particular, because a lot of these businesses will rely on a large buyer being willing to pay a non-China premium,” Sturrock said.

Rounds 1 and 2 funded projects include South Australian solar panel manufacturer Tindo Solar, Sydney-based solar technology company 5B and China-headquartered Sunman, founded by solar pioneer and University of New South Wales (UNSW) alumnus Dr Zhengrong Shi, which is building a 500 MW per annum solar module manufacturing facility in the Hunter Valley, New South Wales (NSW) backed by $171 million in federal and state government funding.

The Australian Renewable Energy Agency (ARENA) is delivering the $850 million Solar Sunshot program, launched in March 2024, to support innovation in Australia’s solar PV manufacturing industry.

item.title: EVX unveils Australian-made DC fast charger for EVs
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Australian electric vehicle infrastructure company EVX is expanding into locally manufactured DC fast-charging technology, unveiling plans to launch a new 40–50 kW pole-mounted charger early next year.
item.content:encoded:
Sydney-headquartered electric vehicle (EV) charger manufacturer EVX has announced plans to launch a new pole-mounted DC fast charger specifically designed for Australian conditions, building on its existing kerbside AC charging technology.

“We have already demonstrated that public EV charging infrastructure can be designed and manufactured locally and deployed at meaningful scale,” EVX Chief Executive Officer Andrew Forster said.

“Polecharger Rapid is the next step, taking that capability into DC charging and creating a product specifically for the places and conditions in which Australian councils, networks and communities need it to operate.”

EVX said the new Australian-designed and manufactured product will complement its existing AC pole-mounted charging technology, including the 22 kW dual-charging Polecharger, providing EV drivers with a faster charging option.

“Unlike AC kerbside chargers, where charging speeds are generally limited by the vehicle’s onboard charger to 7–11 kW, or sometimes 22 kW, DC charging bypasses this limitation and enables compatible vehicles to receive power at significantly higher rates,” the company said.

“At 40–50kW, Polecharger Rapid is designed to provide a faster charging option for public locations, with compatible EVs potentially able to charge in an hour or less, depending on battery capacity and charging conditions.”

EVX said it is currently progressing detailed engineering, certification and manufacturing details for Polecharger Rapid, adding it plans to release further technical specifications, manufacturing and deployment details closer to a commercial release.

The company is targeting initial deployments in early 2027 in strategically selected locations across urban activity centres and regional and rural communities.

Forster said the new Polecharger Rapid marks the next stage in EVX’s Australian manufacturing program and will build on the company’s established manufacturing and supply-chain capabilities.

“Local manufacturing is not simply about where the hardware gets made. It is about retaining the engineering knowledge, intellectual property, supply-chain capability and technical support required to keep critical infrastructure operating over its full life,” he said. “We want Australian customers to have an Australian manufacturer standing behind the product.”

The unveiling of the new product comes as the uptake of EVs in Australia continues to accelerate.

A record 157,957 EVs were sold across Australia in the first six months of 2026, a 117% increase on the same period last year, according to the Electric Vehicle Council.

EVs accounted for one in four new cars sold in the first half of 2026, with their market share more than doubling from 12.1% in the first half of 2025 to 25.8% over the same period this year.
